newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Brixton surprised by NAV drop.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Brixton surprised by NAV drop.

text.p: Brixton Estate Plc said on Thursday it had been surprised by the size of the drop in its net asset value (NAV) per share it announced as part of its 1996 results.
While the British property company's pre-tax profit rose 2.8 percent to 36.12 million stg from 35.14 million stg, its NAV dropped to 181 pence per share from 188 pence.
"We are happy with all the numbers apart from the big one which is the net asset value," Steven Owen, Brixton's finance director told Reuters, adding that the market had not expected the drop.
"I certainly hadn't expected such a decrease," Owen said, adding that he had known there would be a fall due to the effects of the appreciation of sterling on Brixton's Belgian and German portfolios.
But he said he had not known that the end figure of the valuation of Brixton's properties would be 11.7 million stg lower. The group's portfolio was valued at 880 million stg at the end of 1996.
Owen said that at the end of 1996 Brixton had had a number of large empty office buildings, one of these had recently been let and as a result an improvement in its valuation could be expected.
"We have seen more enquiries for office space so as the economy recovers, as soon as these buildings become let out there will be a correction in values on the office sector," he added.

Owen said Brixton was moving back towards its niche markets of industrial property and warehouses in the south east of Britain but would still maintain key office buildings in major provincial towns around the south east of the country.

In the medium term Brixton aims to withdraw completely from overseas markets and become a 100 percent British company. Owen said it had largely withdrawn from Australia, France and the U.S. and hoped to finish this by the end of 1997.

He said the company would like to have started the divestment process from Germany and Belgium by 1999 when the retirement of the two local directors in those markets would make the timing convenient.
But if those markets improved substantially before this then the group "might be tempted to dispose of one or two properties".

Looking to its prospects for 1997, Owen said the key to Brixton improving its NAV figure was to let its vacant space. He said properties let during 1996 performed very well compared with those let in 1995.
"One way of getting the NAV up is through letting property," he said, adding that he thought growth in the market should assist a rise in valuations.
Another factor likely to lead to an improved NAV was a growing economy and increasing foreign investment in Britain. "We've been letting space to all sorts of foreign companies here," he said.
"That has already started to reflect a shortage in industrial space in the greater London area and the south east in general," he added.

Brixton's shares were marked down by 17.5 pence at 185 pence at 1015 GMT. Owen said the initial fall in the share price was greater than he had expected but added he had not yet spoken to analysts about the results.
